prompt_version: s5-extract-facts-v2 (adapted from Paleo Atlas extract-facts-v3; v2 after Sofía's S5 review)

facts.statement: The researchers used a mouse model of Saethre-Chotzen syndrome to measure skull and brain shapes from birth until two weeks old.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: While normal mice kept their front skull seam open, every mutant mouse had that seam fully closed by day 14.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: Mutant mice started with a shortened front-to-back skull width, which developed into a distinct short-and-wide head shape by day 7.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: The abnormal head shape in mutant mice was linked to the widening of specific back-of-the-head skull seams.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: The back parts of the mutant mice's brains bulged upward and backward between days 7 and 14, happening a bit later than the skull changes.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: The authors suggest that the brain bulging is caused by pressure from the fused front skull seam and might be pushing the back skull seams apart.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: Eventually, the widened back skull seams returned to normal size through extra growth of a specific bone in that area.
facts.subject: animals
